Abstract
Background Poxviruses are a diverse group of pathogens with significant implications for both human and animal 
health. Ticks, as hematophagous arthropods, are capable of switching hosts during their life cycle. Although previous

research has suggested the potential for parapoxviral transmission via ticks, the poxviral transmission dynamics 
remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the role of ticks as vectors.
Methods Tick samples were collected from western China, followed by metagenomic sequencing. The diversity of 
potential blood-feeding hosts and the prevalence of poxviruses were assessed using BWA. Poxviral sequences were 
assembled using MetaSPAdes and TGICL, and phylogenetic analysis was conducted to examine the origin of prevalent 
poxviruses and the unblasted poxviral fragments in ticks.
Results A total of 61 poxvirus species across 22 genera were identified, with 387 distinct poxviral sequences 
assembled. Of these, viral and host abundance were relatively higher in Tibet than in samples from Shaanxi and 
Gansu. Notably, unblasted gene fragments were identified within the assembled poxviral genomes, originating 
from a broad range of hosts, including mammals (e.g., rodents), fish, and arthropods. Phylogenetic analysis of the 
parapoxviruses revealed ongoing mutations, particularly in the Parapoxvirus orf, suggesting an increase in adaptability 
and potential pathogenicity. The results indicate that environmental factors such as altitude, host availability and host 
sensitivity may significantly shape viral diversity and transmission dynamics.
Conclusions Ticks may contribute to the ecological circulation of poxviruses by switching hosts during their life 
cycle, potentially influencing viral genetic diversity. It underscores the risks of zoonotic spillover, particularly in regions 
with frequent human-animal interactions.
Keywords Poxvirus, Tick, Host, Evolution, Gene gain
The silent spread: uncovering the diversity 
and evolution of poxviruses in ticks across 
Western China’s host landscapes

Introduction

As specialized blood-sucking arthropods, ticks have 
a broad host range and serve as significant vectors for 
transmitting bacterial, viral, and other zoonotic pathogens [1]. Similar to other arthropods, the distribution 
and density of ticks are significantly affected by climate 
change and human activities. Climate warming and 
human-induced land use changes, in particular, expand 
the range and population size of ticks, thereby directly 
contributing to the transmission and spread of tick-borne 
zoonotic diseases [2–4].
Poxviruses are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA 
viruses capable of infecting a wide range of animals, 
including mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, and insects [5]. 
Within the family Poxviridae, certain species of the genera Orthopoxvirus (OPV), Parapoxvirus, Molluscipoxvirus, and Yatapoxvirus can infect humans, and most of 
these are zoonotic [6–8]. The genus OPV, represented by 
Orthopoxvirus monkeypox (MPV), has garnered heightened global attention with the MPV clade II pandemic 
in 2022, which was largely transmitted within the MSM 
(men who have sex with men) population, and the high 
lethality rate (3%) of the MPV clade I pandemic in 2024 
[9]. In July 2022 and August 2024, the WHO declared 
the mpox outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) twice, indicating that OPV 
has imposed a significant disease burden on global public health and requires heightened attention. In addition, 
previous studies have found evidence in poxviral genome 
that poxviruses could continually capture genes from 
their hosts, co-infecting viruses, and even the environment during the transmission process, and would retain 
or discard these genes through adaptive mutations [10–
13]. These processes have been observed in select poxvirus genera and remain under investigation for many 
others. Consequently, studying the poxviral evolution 
could not only reveal viral evolutionary patterns but also

aid in future prevention and control efforts by anticipating changes in virulence genes.
China is home to various climate types, with Gansu, 
Shaanxi, and Tibet encompassing nearly all of them, 
including subtropical monsoon, temperate monsoon, 
temperate continental, and alpine climates. This diversity makes ticks collected from western China representative of the overall tick population across the country. 
Additionally, these regions, spanning longitudes 78°25’–
111°15’E and latitudes 26°50’–42°57’N, feature a broad 
range of altitudinal gradients (600–4,500  m) and host 
a variety of ecosystems, such as alpine meadows, plateau wetlands, glacial tundra, alpine forests, and deserts. 
These areas, characterized by rich biodiversity, support 
numerous vertebrates, arthropods, and microorganisms. 
A significant proportion of farmers in these provinces are 
involved in animal husbandry, exposing them to a broad 
spectrum of zoonotic diseases, including Coronaviridae, 
Flaviviridae, Hepeviridae, Herpesviridae, and Poxviridae 
[14–16]. Moreover, the tundra of the Tibetan Plateau is 
home to a diverse array of potential pathogens, presenting unique biosecurity risks [17]. This makes arthropod-based virus surveillance in these areas particularly 
important.
Hematophagous arthropods, particularly ticks, have 
been confirmed as competent vectors for several poxvirus transmission between mammalian hosts through 
interrupted feeding behaviors [18–21]. This mechanical transmission mechanism enables viral dissemination 
across host and geographic barriers during blood meal 
acquisition. However, no study has comprehensively 
described the diversity and abundance of different poxvirus species in ticks from western China. To better understand the host diversity during the tick life cycle, as well 
as the diversity, evolution, and transmission of poxviruses in ticks in western China, ticks were collected from 
three provinces: Gansu, Shaanxi, and Tibet. Metagenomic sequencing was conducted on these ticks to obtain

information about their potential blood-feeding hosts 
and poxvirome. From this study, we revealed the host 
dynamics of ticks in these regions, explored the interrelationships between tick-associated poxviruses and their 
hosts, and examined the evolution and transmission of 
poxviruses in ticks.
Methods and materials
Sample collection
Between April and August 2022, and in July 2023, ticks 
were collected from rural areas in three provinces, 
including Gansu, Shaanxi, and Tibet. Parasitic ticks were 
carefully gathered using tweezers from the body surfaces 
of domesticated sheep, cattle, and camels, while questing 
ticks were sampled from grasslands using the flag-dragging method. The collected ticks’ surfaces were cleaned 
by 75% ethyl alcohol, and were initially identified through 
morphological analysis conducted by experts trained 
in the field [22]. Subsequently, the samples underwent 
amplification and sequencing using primers targeting 
the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) 
gene to achieve final identification. Ticks were grouped 
into sampling pools based on factors such as species, 
gender, collection location, sampling time, and bloodfeeding status.
Library preparation and sequencing
Ticks were individually washed with sterile RNA/DNAfree PBS solution according to their sample groupings, 
and then homogenized in RLT solution under liquid 
nitrogen. Total DNA was extracted following the manufacturer’s instructions with the Ex-DNA/RNA nucleic 
acid extraction kit (TIAN LONG, China). DNA libraries 
Wang et al. Virology Journal (2025) 22:214 Page 3 of 13
were prepared using the QIAseq® FX DNA Library Kit 
(Qiagen, Germany) and then subjected to paired-end 
(150-bp) sequencing on a NovaSeq sequencer (Illumina, 
Inc., San Diego, CA).
The annotation and analysis of ticks’ potential bloodfeeding hosts
Low-quality and short reads were filtered from the raw 
data using fastp (v0.23.4) [23] to obtain clean reads. 
The clean reads were then mapped to the DNA barcode 
database, which was downloaded from the Barcode of

Life Data Systems (BOLD systems), using the BurrowsWheeler Alignment tool (BWA) (v0.7.17-r1188) [24]. 
Ticks commonly feed on mammals, birds, reptiles, and 
amphibians. Reads annotated to these classes were filtered and defined as potential blood-feeding hosts during the tick’s life cycle. The abundance of tick hosts in 
each sampling pool was standardized quantifying by calculating the number of reads matched per million total 
clean reads in the library, thus eliminating the effect of 
sequencing depth.
Based on the taxonomy of tick hosts identified in each 
pool, the hosts were categorized into families, orders, and 
classes, and their total abundances were calculated. Host 
visualization by order and class for each pool was performed using the ‘ComplexHeatmap’ package (v2.16.0) in 
R (v4.3.0). Box plots representing the four orders of hosts 
detected across all samples were generated using the 
‘ggplot2’ package (v3.5.1) in R. Non-parametric KruskalWallis test was conducted in SPSS Statistics (v27.0.1.0) to 
assess between-group differences in the abundance of the 
four classes across all samples, followed by Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction to further investigate pairwise between-group differences among the four 
classes. In the investigation of mammalian host diversity 
in ticks, the mean values of mammalian hosts were calculated separately by family and order across all samples. 
The top 30 families, ranked by mean abundance, were 
selected and visualized using the ‘ggplot2’ package in R. 
Furthermore, based on these top 30 families, the ‘ggpubr’ 
package (v0.6.0) in R was employed to depict the proportional mean abundances of their respective orders.
Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA) was conducted 
to assess the variations in blood-feeding hosts of ticks 
gathered from diverse geographical locations and species, 
utilizing host abundance data from each sampling pool. 
The PCoA outcomes were visualized via the ‘ggplot2’

package. Additionally, the ‘vegan’ package (v2.6.8) in R 
was employed to execute the adonis test, evaluating the 
differences in blood-feeding hosts among ticks from distinct geographical locations and species.
The annotation and analysis of viral contigs
Clean reads were aligned to the Nucleotide Sequence 
Database using BWA, and the abundance of each poxvirus was quantified by the reads matched per million total 
reads. Visualization of poxvirus abundance in each pool 
was achieved using the ‘ComplexHeatmap’ package in R. 
PCoA was conducted to assess the variations in tick-associated poxvirus gathered from diverse geographical locations and tick species. The results were visualized via the 
‘ggplot2’ package, and the ‘vegan’ package was employed 
to execute the adonis test, evaluating the differences in 
poxviruses among ticks from distinct geographical locations and species.
The association analysis of ticks’ blood-feeding hosts and 
tick-associared OPVs
Due to the strong host specificity of mammalian poxviruses and the lack of direct evidence for their ability to 
replicate in ticks, mammalian poxviruses detected in 
ticks are likely derived from the ticks’ blood-feeding 
hosts. Thus, the abundance of mammalian blood-feeding hosts (categorized into families) during the ticks’ 
life cycle were used as the independent variable and the 
abundance of OPVs in ticks as the dependent variable to 
perform partial least squares regression (PLS) analyses 
using SIMCA (v14.1). This approach assessed the relationship between mammalian blood-feeding hosts and 
OPVs, followed by extracting the Variable Importance in 
Projection (VIP) index for each host. Mammalian hosts 
with VIP values greater than one were filtered and visualized using the ‘ggplot2’ package in R. To further validate 
the correlation between mammalian poxviruses and tick 
blood-feeding hosts, we conducted a Spearman correlation analysis between poxvirus abundance and the 
abundance of tick blood-feeding hosts using the ‘psych’

package in R (v2.4.12). The Spearman correlation coefficients and corresponding p-values were visualized using 
the ‘pheatmap’ package (v1.0.12) in R.
The assembly and identification of poxviral contigs
Clean reads were mapped to nucleotide (NT) library for 
species annotation using Kraken2 (v2.1.3) [25], and reads 
annotated as poxviruses were filtered out. annotated to 
poxviruses. The reads identified as poxviruses were de 
novo assembled into contigs using MetaSPAdes (v3.15.5) 
[26], followed by further extension assembly with TIGR 
Gene Indices clustering tools (TGICL) (v2.1) [27]. 
These assembled contigs were aligned against 46 reference sequences of chordopoxviruses using blastn with 
parameters set to an e-value of ≤1×10−5 and a length of 
≥45  bp. For the fragments failing alignment with poxviral reference sequences, we implemented a length 
threshold of 45  bp. Sequences exceeding this threshold 
were retained and operationally classified as unblasted 
Wang et al. Virology Journal (2025) 22:214 Page 4 of 13
fragments within the assembled contigs. However, if the 
total length of the unblasted fragments exceeds twothirds of the assembled contig’s sequence after alignment 
with the poxvirus, these fragments will be discarded.
The fragments within the assembled contigs that could 
be aligned with poxviruses were uploaded to NCBI’s 
Standard Nucleotide BLAST (BLASTn) online platform. 
The comparison was conducted against the nucleotide 
collection (nr/nt) database using the BLAST algorithm 
with the parameter set to somewhat similar sequences 
(blastn) and an e-value threshold of ≤1×10−5. The 
matched results were subsequently aligned using mafft 
(v7.520). The aligned sequences were imported into 
MEGA-X software to construct a phylogenetic tree using 
the Neighbor-Joining method with a bootstrap value of 
1,000 and a substitution model based on the maximum

composite likelihood model. The resulting phylogenetic 
tree was refined and visualized using iTOL [28]. Subsequently, the nucleotide sequences were translated into 
amino acid sequences using MEGA-X, and these amino 
acid sequences were aligned with ClustalW. Differential 
sites in the aligned amino acid sequences were identified, 
visualized, and presented using GeneDoc software.
The unblasted fragments from those assembled contigs 
lengths ranking in the top 60 were subjected to BLASTn 
analysis through the NCBI online platform, using identical parameters as previously described. All species 
matched by the unblasted fragments in each assembled 
contig were recorded separately. The ‘UpSetR’ package (v1.4.0) in R was employed to visualize the enriched 
classes in the comparison results of unblasted fragments 
from assembled contigs. Furthermore, both the invertebrate phyla and the classes within the phylum Chordata 
of the enriched species identified in these comparison 
results were visualized using the ‘UpSetR’ package and 
the ‘ggplot2’ package.
Results
Shaanxi, Gansu, and Tibet were selected as tick collection positions and 234 ticks were collected in total. 
Among these ticks, 35 were cattle-parasitic ticks, 115 
were sheep-parasitic ticks, 14 were camel-parasitic ticks, 
and 70 were questing ticks. All ticks were identified both 
morphologically and molecularly to classify their species. 
Ultimately, they were found belonging to Dermacentor 
marginatus (D. marginatus), Haemaphysalis longicornis
(Ha. longicornis), Haemaphysalis tibetensis (Ha. tibetensis), Hyalomma asiaticum (Hy. asiaticum), and Ixodes 
ovatus (I. ovatus). The 234 collected ticks were divided 
into 43 sampling pools based on their species, collected 
locations, and parasitic status. The information for each 
sampling is presented in Fig.  1 and Table S1. A total of

363  million raw reads were generated through metagenomic sequencing of these sampling pools, and 357 million clean reads were retained for further analysis.
Fig. 1 Sampling positions, species, and parasitic status of ticks’ sampling pools. Each red dot indicates the collection position of ticks within a sampling 
pool. Different colors and animal silhouettes are used to represent the species and parasitic status of ticks collected at each location. All animal silhouettes 
were obtained from the Phylopic website. To distinguish the hosts of parasitic ticks when collected from potential blood-feeding hosts obtained by mapping the BOLD database, parasitic status was used to designate both parasitic and questing ticks at the time of collection
Wang et al. Virology Journal (2025) 22:214 Page 5 of 13
Sequences from the classes Amphibia, Aves, Mammalia, and Reptilia were taxonomically identified by comparing the sequencing data with the BOLD database 
(Table S2). Notably, the abundance of mammalian hosts 
is higher than that of the other three classes throughout 
the lifecycle of ticks in this study (Fig. 2a and Figure S1a). 
Non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test indicated a statistically significant difference (p<0.001) in the mean abundance of hosts among the four classes within the ticks. 
The Mann-Whitney U test with Bonferroni correction 
further revealed that the mean abundance of mammals 
was significantly different (p<0.001) compared to each of 
the other three classes. Ticks collected in this study were 
more inclined to feed on mammalian blood during their 
previous life cycles. Among all the mammalian hosts of 
ticks, the family Sciuridae from Rodentia had the highest average abundance, followed by the family Bovidae 
from Artiodactyla, the family Muridae from Rodentia, 
and the family Cercopithecidae from Primates (Fig. 2b). 
According to the species taxonomic information, all 
families that ranked in the top 30 in terms of average 
abundance belonged to a total of 10 orders. Based on 
the average abundance of species from these orders in

ticks, the top six orders are Rodentia, Artiodactyla, Primates, Carnivora, Chiroptera and Eulipotyphla (Fig. 2b). 
PCoA revealed significant differences in the hosts of ticks 
from different geographical locations (Adonis, p=0.001) 
and different species (Adonis, p=0.001) (Fig. 2c and d). 
Although both p-values were equal to 0.001, the differences between groups of tick hosts from different species were smaller than those from different geographic 
locations, as observed in the images. Additionally, higher 
host abundance was detected in samples from Tibet compared to those from other geographical origins (Figure 
S1a and Figure S1b).
Following the alignment of clean reads to the nucleotide sequence database, a total of 17,767 reads corresponding to chordopoxviral gene fragments were 
identified, encompassing 51 species across 18 genera. 
Additionally, 1,169 reads pertaining to entomopoxviral 
gene fragments were detected, representing 10 species 
across three known genera and one unidentified genus 
(Table S3). The abundance of the 61 poxviruses in each 
sample can be visualized in the heatmap, which reveals 
significant differences among virus species from samples originating from different geographical locations 
(Fig.  3a). Notably, relatively high poxvirus abundance 
was observed in ticks from Tibet, with one sampling pool 
containing Ha. tibetensis showing higher abundances of 
Yatapoxvirus tanapox and Suipoxvirus swinepox compared to others. Ticks from Shaanxi showed a high abundance of Avipoxvirus canarypox and Macropopoxvirus 
mfuliginosuspox compared to other regions. Additionally, three sampling pools collected from sheep in Gansu 
contained a high abundance of Parapoxvirus orf (ORFV). 
PCoA revealed significant differences in poxviral abundance in ticks from different geographic locations 
(Adonis, p=0.001) and among different species (Adonis,

p=0.001) (Fig. 3b and c).
PLS regression (R2X=0.69, R2Y=0.56, Q2=0.39) was 
used to explore hosts that play an important role in the 
abundance of OPVs in ticks, and 80 families with a VIP 
score greater than 1 were identified as potentially important (Fig.  3d). Among them, 15 families belong to the 
order Rodentia, representing the largest proportion of 
all mammalian hosts of interest. Of the remaining families, 13 belong to the order Primates, 9 to Artiodactyla, 9 
to Carnivora, and 8 to Diprotodontia. A Spearman correlation analysis between mammophilic poxviruses and 
mammals from the top 30 families with the highest average abundance revealed that, among all mammals with 
significant positive correlations to OPV, the highest percentage belonged to the order Rodentia (Figure S2).
A total of 387 sequences (≥300  bp) were assembled 
from poxviral reads, with one sequence exceeding 1  kb 
in length and 125 sequences exceeding 500  bp (Table 
S4). In examining the differences between poxviruses in 
ticks and 46 chordopoxviral reference sequences (Table 
S5), we identified multiple sequences that matched the 
genus Parapoxvirus with an e-value of 0, indicating these 
sequences likely reflect ingestion during blood-feeding rather than endogenous replication (Table S4). For 
example, an assembled sequence named ‘Contig 1’, with 
a length of 1,171 bp, matched the 122,627−121,462 fragment of the Orf virus reference strain (NC_005336.1) 
with an e-value of 0. As the matching fragment contained the ORFVgORF122 and ORFVgORF121 genes, 
the corresponding sequences in Contig 1 were extracted 
separately, and phylogenetic analyses were performed 
for each gene (Fig. 4a and b), along with comparisons of

their respective coding amino acid sites (Fig. 4c and d). 
Notably, the Orf virus strains closely clustering with the 
two fragments of Contig 1 originate from China, and the 
142nd amino acid site of the 595–1,196 fragment of the 
assembled Contig 1 sequence differs from other strains 
prevalent in China.
The species which the unblasted fragments of the longest 60 contigs had matched were diverse (Table S6). 
At the class level, unblasted fragments from multiple 
contigs were successfully aligned with sequences from 
Mammalia, Actinopteri, Insecta, Clitellata, Polychaeta, 
Gastropoda, and Bivalvia (Fig. 5a). Given the closer evolutionary relationship between vertebrates and humans, 
we concentrated on gene fragments derived from vertebrate genomes within poxviruses. Consequently, when 
constructing the upset plot at the species level, our focus 
was on classes within the phylum Chordata, as well as 
other phyla that were previously mentioned. Among

(Fig. 5b).
Discussion
In this study, we employed metagenomic sequencing to 
analyze 43 tick sampling pools from Shaanxi, Gansu, and 
Tibet, facilitating an in-depth exploration of the tick life 
cycle and the diversity and evolution of tick-associated

poxviruses in western China. Our results revealed significant geographic variation in host diversity and the associated poxviruses throughout the tick life cycle. Notably, 
we observed that parapoxviruses in China are undergoing 
continuous mutation, underscoring the need for vigilant 
monitoring. Additionally, our analysis of the unblasted 
fragments within the tick-associated poxvirus sequence 
suggests that these poxviruses may be evolving through a 
process of gene acquisition from diverse hosts, including 
mammals, bony fishes, and arthropods.
Ticks are hematophagous ectoparasites that feed on the 
blood of mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians. Most 
species within the genus Ixodes are multi-host ticks, with 
their larval, nymphal, and adult stages parasitizing a variety of hosts. These ticks exhibit distinct host preferences 
depending on species. All five tick species collected in 
this study were mammalianophilic, primarily feeding on 
small mammals such as rats and hedgehogs, as well as 
larger mammals like cows and sheep [29–31]. These findings were consistent with in vivo host-source sequence 
comparisons conducted in ticks, which indicated that 
mammalian hosts dominate throughout the tick life 
cycle. The six most abundant host orders identified in

Wang et al. Virology Journal (2025) 22:214 Page 10 of 13
ticks—Rodentia, Artiodactyla, Primates, Carnivora, Chiroptera, and Eulipotyphla—align with known patterns of

host distribution. Wild small mammals, such as rodents, 
bats, and shrews, as well as economically significant 
mammals like raccoons and minks, are not only geographically close to humans but also act as reservoirs for 
a wide range of viruses with potential for host-jumping 
[32–34]. These animals are increasingly recognized as 
significant sources of emerging zoonotic viruses.
As widely distributed and specialized blood-feeding 
arthropods, ticks are capable of switch hosts throughout 
their life cycle. This adaptability, particularly in urbanized regions, allows ticks to harbor and transmit viruses 
from small mammals and livestock species closely associated with human activities [35, 36]. Such host-switching 
behavior promotes cross-species transmission, increasing the likelihood of zoonotic spillover events into human 
populations. Importantly, viruses that acquire adaptive 
mutations during these host switches can rapidly emerge 
in densely populated human environments, posing significant risks to public health [37].
In our study, we detected gene fragments from chordopoxviruses corresponding to 44 known and 7 previously 
unidentified species within tick samples, suggesting that 
ticks may act as mechanical vectors for poxviral transmission. This finding indicates the potential for both 
cross-host and cross-species transmission of poxviruses 
via ticks. Although we did not confirm the replication of 
poxviruses within ticks in our experiments, the viruses 
were able to passively retain in tick cells for up to 35 days 
[38], implying that poxviruses may be transmitted to new 
hosts during ticks’ blood-feeding activities. Prior studies have confirmed that the Capripoxvirus lumpyskinpox
(LSDV), the Leporipoxvirus myxoma, and various species 
of the genus Avipoxvirus can be mechanically transmitted by blood-feeding arthropods, including ticks, fleas, 
and mosquitoes [18, 39, 40]. More surprisingly, LSDV 
acquired by ticks from infected hosts can be transmitted vertically to their offspring, thereby perpetuating 
the infection in the host population [21]. These observations strengthen the hypothesis that blood-sucking

arthropods, particularly ticks, could play a critical role in 
facilitating the cross-host transmission of poxviruses and 
contribute to their spread.
Interactions between ticks’ blood-feeding hosts, tickassociated poxviruses and ticks varied significantly across 
geographical landscapes in this study. In particular, 
the higher abundance of poxviruses and blood-feeding 
hosts in ticks collected from Tibet compared to those 
from Shaanxi and Gansu underscores the influence of 
ecological factors such as altitude and climate. In Tibet, 
the uniquely cold, arid, and low-oxygen climatic conditions compel ticks to reduce their metabolic activities, 
potentially prolonging their life cycle [41]. Furthermore, 
to adapt more effectively to the extreme cold, ticks may 
remain attached to their hosts longer in cold climates, 
enhancing the potential for gene exchange or viral persistence [42]. We hypothesize that the aforementioned 
factors may collectively contribute to the high prevalence 
of host-derived gene fragments in ticks, and might potentially facilitating the acquisition of additional poxviruses 
from the host. Specifically, the longer a tick parasitizes 
a host, the slower its metabolic rate becomes, leading 
to the retention of more host-derived genetic material. 
Nevertheless, the substantial number of poxviral reads 
identified in ticks from Tibet, as well as the high quantity 
of reads originating from the blood-feeding hosts, may 
also be attributed to sampling bias. This could be due to 
the relatively small sample size of ticks collected in Tibet 
and the geographically limited collection area. Regardless, these findings still suggest that ticks and other 
hematophagous arthropods in plateau regions, such as 
Tibet, may play a significant role in the transmission of 
emerging zoonotic viruses, thereby warranting serious 
consideration.
The traditional naming of poxviruses based on their 
first-identified host species is increasingly being questioned. Research indicates that the host in which virus 
was initially identified is not necessarily its natural reservoir. This is exemplified by OPV, such as MPV, which

have attracted global attention due to their recent outbreaks. While these viruses were first identified in a 
wide range of host species, it is now widely accepted 
that Rodentia—particularly wild rodents—serve as the 
primary natural reservoir hosts for many OPV species 
[43–45]. Our findings further support this hypothesis, as 
members of Rodentia represented the highest proportion 
of families associated with OPV in ticks. However, this 
result is influenced by the abundance of tick blood-feeding hosts in the habitat. The association between OPV 
and natural rodent hosts in western China remains to be 
confirmed through further experiments. These observations reinforce the necessity for enhanced surveillance 
of wild rodent populations to monitor and control the 
spread of re-emerging poxviruses like MPV.
The ORFV, a zoonotic poxvirus prevalent in small 
ruminants such as goats and sheep, is widely distributed across East Asia, including China [46, 47]. In this 
study, we detected a high abundance of ORFV in two 
pools of Hy. asiaticum and one pool of D. marginatus, 
all collected from sheep in Gansu province. These findings suggest that an ORFV epidemic occurred in sheep 
in Gansu between April and August 2022. Additionally, 
the identification of mutation sites in the ORFV sequence 
distinct from other strains, indicates that the domestic 
ORFV is still undergoing evolution, which may lead to 
changes in its virulence and pathogenicity. Although the 
function of the protein encoded by the ORFVgORF121

gene remains unknown, it can be hypothesized that the 
ongoing mutation could enhance the viral adaptability to 
ruminant hosts and potentially increase its risk to human 
health. Previous studies have highlighted that east and 
south Asia are hotspots for ORFV transmission, where 
several genes in the viral genome are subject to positive 
selection pressures [48], further supporting the urgent 
need for improved ORFV surveillance, rapid isolation of 
infected animals, and strategies to prevent cross-species 
transmission.

The Chordopoxvirinae subfamily may have evolved 
from Entomopoxvirinae [13], or both may share a common ancestor in a bilaterian Metazoa infectious poxvirus [49]. As these viruses have evolved, they continue 
to acquire genes from their hosts to counteract antiviral 
defenses [13]. Additionally, under selective pressure, they 
lose non-essential genes and introduce early stop mutations to optimize host resource utilization and promote 
coexistence [50]. The evolution of poxviruses is marked 
by frequent gene capture, and their genomes will retain 
some genes from their hosts during the evolutionary 
process. Some genes of host origin that were parasitized 
by viruses in the early stages of evolution may have only 
small fragments remaining in their genomes, whereas 
hosts experienced by viruses in their more recent evolutionary history may have more complete gene fragments 
remaining. Regardless of the length of the residual fragments, however, the presence of these genes can help 
in the exploration of the evolutionary history of poxviruses. For instance, the presence of the Sauria SINE gene 
from Echis ocellatus in the genome of the Orthopoxvirus 
taterapox suggests potential historical cross-class infection of reptilian species by this virus and related OPVs 
[51]. In this study, the results further support the idea 
of extensive host switching during the evolutionary history of poxviruses, with many poxviruses acquiring genes 
from a variety of host species. We identified several 
unblasted fragments within the assembled chordopoxviral sequences that did not match any known poxviral 
reference, suggesting historical gene sharing events or 
sequence convergence with hosts such as mammals, bony 
fishes, and arthropods; however, the possibility of contamination or sequencing artifacts cannot be excluded. 
This horizontal gene transfer likely occurred through 
mobile genetic elements, such as long interspersed 
nuclear element-1 (LINE-1), which mediate retrotransposition of mammalian-derived mRNA into poxvirus

genomes [52]. However, the matches of unblasted fragments to potential hosts do not completely eliminate 
other possible explanations, such as contamination or the 
assembly of artifacts.
The presence of the unblasted fragments in the chordopoxviruses assembled in this study, which align with 
fish species, supports the hypothesis that poxviruses 
may have evolved from aquatic hosts before adapting 
to terrestrial environments, and this hypothesis merits targeted virome studies in aquatic hosts. Fish, being 
the most diverse group among vertebrates, may harbor 
poxviruses comparable in diversity to those found in 
mammals, though very few fish poxviruses have been 
identified thus far [5, 53, 54]. Our study thus opens 
the door to the discovery of previously unknown fish 
poxviruses, which may hold key insights into poxviral 
evolution. Furthermore, the identification of arthropodderived gene fragments in the poxviral genomes raises 
the possibility of genetic recombination between poxviruses and entomopoxviruses, suggesting a complex evolutionary history that warrants further investigation.
However, this study has several limitations. The study 
relied solely on tick metagenome sequencing data, which 
influenced the results due to challenges in completely 
removing contamination during data analysis, difficulties in eliminating assembly artifacts during poxvirus 
assembly, and the oversensitivity of the virus sequences 
and tick blood-feeding host identification methods, all 
of which may lead to false-positive results. Additionally, the study was limited to tick sequencing data and 
did not incorporate relevant experiments to validate the 
hypotheses derived from the analysis. Future refinement 
of experimental methods will be necessary to confirm the 
findings more robustly.
Conclusions
In this study, we collected a total of 234 ticks from Tibet, 
Gansu, and Shaanxi provinces in China and 43 metagenomic sequencing datasets from five tick species were 
obtained. Our results revealed the transmission, prevalence, and mutation of multiple poxviruses, particularly parapoxviruses, in the western regions of China.

Notably, in Tibet, the unique plateau environment contributed to a higher abundance of both poxviruses and 
blood-feeding hosts in the collected ticks compared to 
other regions. Additionally, the assembled chordopoxviral sequences contained various unblasted fragments of 
genes from mammals, bony fishes, arthropods, and other 
species, illustrating the genetic complexity and possible 
host associations in the evolutionary history of poxviruses. Influenced by interactions between viruses, hosts, 
vectors, and the environment, poxviruses are shaped 
by continuously acquiring genes and undergoing adaptive mutations, which may facilitate changes in their 
virulence, transmission potential, and even host jumping 
ability. By utilizing tick metagenomic sequencing data to 
connect ticks, poxviruses, and hosts, this study not only 
underscore the need for continued surveillance of zoonotic poxviruses in vector populations but also explores 
the potential evolutionary dynamics of these viruses.
